text.p: The commander of West African peacekeepers in Liberia said on Wednesday the country was completely cleared of landmines and urged refugees to return home ahead of presidential elections in May.
"Anybody can now travel anywhere in the country without any fears of landmines," General Victor Malu, Nigerian commander of the ECOMOG force, said in a broadcast on local radio.

Liberian refugees had returned from neighbouring countries "in good numbers through border villages in the past few days", Malu said, after the last mines were cleared from the world's biggest rubber plantation north of Monrovia.

The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR has earmarked $60 million for repatriating and resettling refugees, who are mainly in Ivory Coast and Guinea, regional director Albert-Alain Peters told a news conference on Wednesday.
A massive voluntary repatriation exercise would start in May for people wishing to return to Liberia, he said.

"While the UNHCR does not intend to force Liberians to return home against their will, refugees remaining outside Liberia after the 18-month repatriation period will have to give convincing reasons for their decision to remain," he added.

Liberia was plunged into a bloody civil war in 1989 which killed at least 150,000 people after former warlord and now presidential election front-runner Charles Taylor launched a rebellion from Ivory Coast.
Faction leaders handed in weapons and demobilised in an operation that ended in early February.
Former rebels loyal to Taylor's National Patriotic Front led ECOMOG troops to the last remaining mines in the vast Firestone plantation.
Firestone tyre company recently unveiled plans to re-open the plantation 40 km (25 miles) from Monrovia and resume tapping.
